I’ve been switching from OpenCode to Codex for two weeks now. Its goal feature is incredibly useful and has greatly automated my workflow

Rewritten as a plugin per maintainer feedback — zero core code changes.

The implementation is in PR #28610. How it works:

- A built-in plugin registers `create_goal` / `update_goal` / `get_goal` tools and the `/goal` command
- State is stored in `.opencode/goals.json` (no SQLite migration needed)
- Continuation loop uses the `session.status` idle event + `client.promptAsync()` to inject a `<system-reminder>` prompt for the next LLM turn
- `/goal pause|resume|clear` subcommands handled inline, no LLM call
- 34 tests covering the full plugin lifecycle (18 unit + 16 integration)

The PR is ready for review.

Hi everyone,

I’ve been working on this [`@bojackduy/opencode-loopd`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@bojackduy/opencode-loopd) as a plugin-based implementation that explores much of the same problem space discussed in this issue.

`opencode-loopd` implements a persistent goal and continuation engine rather than a prompt-only `/goal` command. The current implementation includes:

- Persistent goal state
- Automatic continuation when a worker session becomes idle
- Pause, resume, clear, and steering controls
- Turn, failure, no-progress, and timeout limits
- Explicit progress and completion tools available to the worker
- Optional shell-based verification before accepting completion
- Dedicated child sessions for background goals
- Multiple goals that can run independently while the parent session remains interactive

The main architectural difference is that `opencode-loopd` models a goal as a **managed background worker session**, rather than attaching the goal directly to the current OpenCode session.

I do not consider this a replacement for a native implementation. A core implementation still has important advantages that a plugin cannot fully provide, including:

- Canonical server-side goal state
- Official HTTP and SDK APIs
- Shared state across TUI, desktop, and other clients
- Runtime-owned lifecycle and accounting semantics
- A stable goal primitive that other OpenCode integrations can depend on

That said, I wanted to share the project here because it may be useful as a working experiment and as prior art for some of the lifecycle, continuation, verification, and UX questions involved in this feature.

Repository: https://github.com/bojackduy/opencode-loopd  
npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@bojackduy/opencode-loopd

I would particularly appreciate feedback on the trade-offs between the **background child-session model** used by `opencode-loopd` and the **goal-attached-to-current-session model** proposed here.

If any parts of the implementation or design are useful for the native feature, I’d also be happy to discuss them or contribute relevant ideas upstream.

Hey, got a working plugin for this. Tested with gpt-4o, zero core changes.

Two tools: goal (set/status/clear) and loop (add/list/remove).
State in .opencode/harness/. Slash commands /goal, /goal-status, /loop.

Compared to open PRs:

**#45379 (thdxr)** - core implementation with auto-continuation. Ours is a plugin SDK example, no core changes. Different scope.

**#28610 (closed)** - auto-continuation via idle events. Ours does not do that. User drives with slash commands.

**#32743 (draft)** - SQLite + core runtime. Ours is just file-based state.

**[@bojackduy/opencode-loopd](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@bojackduy/opencode-loopd)** - full production plugin with subagents, TUI dashboard, scheduled goals. It's more mature as as a production goal engine (1000+ lines vs our ~90). Mine is just a simple addition for monitoring/retrying tasks here etc.

| | Our plugin | opencode-loopd |
|---|---|---|
| Lines | ~90 | 1000+ |
| Auto-continuation | No | Yes |
| Subagents | No | Yes |
| TUI dashboard | No | Yes |
| Scheduled goals | No | Yes |
| State | Simple JSON | Complex + artifacts |
| License | MIT | AGPL-3.0 |
| Purpose | Example plugin | Production tool |

Free models work because the slash command injects a prompt telling the agent to call the tool. No tool-calling needed from the model side.
